Does lawn care count in this sub? in the past I have pretty much neglected my lawn and it looks like shit so this year I want to get it in shape but want to try and do it as earth friendly as possible. Just wondering if there are any others out there interested in sharing/discussing lawn care tips? I have a lot learn on the subject.

Biggest problems with lawns is that they are often devoid of flowers and can be just as dead as a concrete slabs. Your lawn also needs to be appropriate for your climate. So maybe finding out what are the native grasses in your region and making a small square to get it started might be an interesting endeavor.

You also need to figure out the general health and soil composition of your yard. Some of us live in places where there might be a lot of clay or sand naturally mixed in the soil and that greatly affects what you can do with your yard.

In the meantime. You'll want to research what type of low growing, creeping plants will do well in your yards conditions and regional climate. Things like Red clover are edible and won't get very high and thrive in a variety of climate zones. Thyme and mint can also be used as edible ground cover.

So report back with your climate region and find out what you yard's soil situation.

So your clay area let's leave them be because they could be turned into a seasonal water feature at a later time.

Your rocks are not barren and can support plants. Rocks hold condensation and many shrubs would be happy to grow on them. Once you get one established, the left litter left behind will fertilize the area for new arrivals.

For your yard, looks like wild flowers are gonna be your best bet. You need to start them in a small area. Wild flowers are successful in the meadows because their roots often form a matt that holds more moisture that the soil usually allows. The flowers once established won't need to be watered and should tolerate the dog urine just fine. There is a group or company called American Meadows that sell seeds for your climate specifically.

Whatever you do, get enough seed to plan for bird attrition. Sow and water at night whenever possible and give a protective layer of hay to whatever you plant.

Grass is tricky. It is often grown like a monoculture crop. It "requires" heavy imput to look nice and green. I don't really do anything wild. But here is what I do :

  • set the mower to its highest setting. This makes the soil retain more moisture, giving a more lush lawn.
  • throw any yard waste like weeds or leaves on the lawn. Don't smother it, but it will get mixed in and decompose.
  • let the lawn clippings fall back onto the ground, do not bag them up. This retains more nutrients in the soil. Remove any huge clumps that could smother grass.

Also, don't be afraid of dandelions and clover. They are actually good for the soil, most weeds are. If it looks drab add some compost or manure and aerate if need be. If it's patchy you can seed in the springtime or fall.

Every state has "Extension" offices (usually affiliated with a state university, but I think they're more Gov than Edu), they will know everything there is to know about growing Anything. They will test soil samples for you, tell you what grows best, and may even provide info on steps you can take to make everything "better" (not sure, I've never used the resource, just know it exists). They will almost certainly be the #1 best source of information for you.

Beyond that, the whole "bag clipping, no mulch them, leave the mower at the Highest setting, no clip it close" arguments are more of an issue when the lawn is established. I can tell you that the landscapers I've worked for all mulch everything (no bagging), and that includes fallen leaves, clipping from shrubs/trees, basically Anything organic. And they kept mower heights to the 2~2.5" range, which is middle ground. Down here in the soggy SE, if you left the deck as high as possible, you'd need to cut 2~3 times a week because the moisture content is SO high (I was forced to bag the clippings because they would just coat the deck otherwise as-well, which added an hour to my mow time). Out in the Rockies, I left the deck as high as possible and still only needed to cut every other week... no moisture. "Universal" suggestions just don't work when it comes to this topic. I would start out a little on the high side and see what works best for you in terms of the lawn retaining water but not staying so soggy that it's a bear to mow.

If you have a little more money than time, hiring a "lawn care" company (not the people who mow for you, the people who spray chemicals, TruGreen is a national company) for a year or so ought to get you 90% of the way with nearly zero effort. It's an option I'm debating myself... have one more project that's going to tear up a section of my yard that's in the way First, but I'm thinking about it.
